utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we start hearing the evidence of the first witness, there are a few procedural matters I would like to deal with briefly. The first one is the clarification of guidance on presentation and tendering of evidence. On the 19th of June, the Chamber has e-mailed a courtesy copy of its guidance on presentation and tendering of evidence to the parties, and it -- this guidance is now put on the record. If Mr. Mladic is ... Yes, we then will start. The Chamber will now give additional clarification and will amend its guidance on tendering and presentation of evidence initially provided on the 10th of November, 2011, and clarified an amendment on the 8th of December, 2011; the 23rd of February of 2012; the 29th of March, 2012; and the 24th of April, 2012. On the 3rd of May, the Prosecution expressed some concerns with regard to the Chamber's guidance. The Chamber already addressed many of these concerns in its clarification and amendment of the guidance on the 24th of April and will not repeat that here. In light of the repeated concerns expressed by the Prosecution as well as the Rule 92 ter motions filed since the 24th of April, 2012, the Chamber has decided to review its guidance again to introduce a few amendments and to provide further clarification on its intended approach. The Prosecution requests, among other things, that the Chamber's guidance be, and I quote, "considered a clear expression of the Chamber's preferences with respect to the evidence presented before the Chamber." The Chamber informs the parties that the guidance is meant to provide an indication to both parties as to the strong preferences of the Chamber when it comes to the tendering and presentation of evidence to which it expects both parties to adhere. Upon a showing of good cause, the Chamber may grant the parties leave to depart from the guidance. As the Prosecution requests and as the Chamber has already stated in its prior clarifications, any determination will be made on a case-by-case basis. The Chamber will issue oral or written decisions on the parties' requests for admission into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater and from the bar table. The Chamber will adopt a certain flexibility when implementing the guidance. The most important aspect of the guidance is not the precise time or number limitation that it sets out. Most important is its purpose, namely, to achieve a focused presentation of evidence, including avoiding duplication of evidence and ensuring that the Chamber is not flooded with evidence that the parties anyway do not intend to rely on in the end. The Chamber provides the following clarifications and amendments to the guidance in light of the parties' latest submissions. With regard to the number of witness statements to be tendered with Rule 92 ter witnesses, the Chamber hereby amends the guidance in the following way: In addition to the one witness statement the Chamber will accept, the Chamber will accept one or more additional, short supplemental witness statements either in existence or still to be taken dealing with specific issues or corrections to the original statement. Further, the Chamber amends its guidance with regard to Rule 92 bis, Rule 92 ter, and Rule 92 quater witnesses in the following way: The Chamber will accept two or more witness statements to be tendered pursuant to the mentioned rules, provided that the different statements cover distinct subject matters. With regard to the time allowed for examination-in-chief of Rule 92 ter witnesses, in its Rule 73 bis (C) decision, the Chamber already accepted that the examination of many of these witnesses will take longer than 30 minutes. In fact, the average for the Rule 92 ter witnesses on the Prosecution's witness list is approximately one hour. Therefore, there is no need for the Prosecution to request exceptions to the guidance in this respect, provided that it intends to stay within the time-limit indicated in its witness list as accepted by the Chamber. With regard to the Chamber's preference for witness statements rather than transcripts from previous cases, the Chamber will not in all cases insist that a statement be taken for witnesses who have not previously provided one. The Chamber will carefully consider the reasons provided by a party as to why a witness statement cannot be taken. The mere fact that this may inconvenience the witness to some extent may very well not be sufficient. If the reason is that the witness is not willing to co-operate with the party and that, for example, the witness may not provide the same information in a statement as was provided in testimony from a prior case, the parties should carefully consider whether it is appropriate to present the testimony of such a witness through Rule 92 ter or 92 bis. If the party has reasons to believe that a witness would not stand by his or her testimony in a prior case, the most efficient way to proceed might be to elicit the witness's evidence viva voce. The party might then tender the prior testimony as a previous inconsistent statement pursuant to the case law of the Tribunal. With regard to Rule 92 bis witnesses, if witness statements exist but the party considers that testimony from a previous case would better reflect the witness's evidence and that taking a new statement would re-traumatise or otherwise constitute a heavy burden for the witness, in such circumstances the Chamber will consider the admission of the transcript. In its submissions, the example the Prosecution provided in this respect was Witness Dzenana Sokolovic. This example highlights another aspect that parties should consider before filing a motion pursuant to Rule 92 bis, 92 ter, or 92 quater, namely, the avoidance of overlap between the adjudicated facts of which the Chamber has taken judicial notice and testimony. It appears that adjudicated facts 2317, 2318, and 2319 cover a central part of what the witness is expected to testify about, at least as it is described in the Rule 65 ter summary prepared by the Prosecution. These facts originate from the Dragomir Milosevic judgement. The Chamber in that case based its findings on this incident primarily on Witness Sokolovic's testimony. In essence, the Prosecution has requested that the Chamber take judicial notice of the facts related to this incident and is now requesting to admit into evidence the testimony on which those facts are based. In this same respect, the Chamber also draws the parties' attention to the Rule 92 ter motion for Witness RM007, whose evidence appears to be substantially covered by a number of adjudicated facts, including facts number 460, 462 through 465, 468 through 476, 478 through 480, 1141 through 1144, 1146, 1165 through 1169, 1190 and 1192. The Prosecution subsequently changed this witness from a Rule 92 ter witness to a viva voce witness but the risk of overlap between the adjudicated facts and the witness testimony remains. There might be examples of other Rule 92 ter motions for which such an overlap exists. For each viva voce witness and for each Rule 92 bis, 92 ter, 92 quater, and Rule 94 bis motions, the Chamber expects the parties to carefully review which portions of the anticipated evidence relate to adjudicated facts and which may therefore no longer be necessary and to reduce its evidence accordingly. The Chamber stresses that this should be done prior to any Rule 92 or 94 bis motion being submitted to the Chamber. Should the parties consider it necessary to still present the evidence, the Chamber expects them to clearly explain the need for such duplication. Where I referred to Rule 92, I think I should have referred to Rule 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater. With regard to associated exhibits, the Chamber will adopt a flexible approach as to the exact number of such documents. The Chamber recalls the case law on this matter which allows for the tendering of documents pursuant to 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater if they form an inseparable and indispensable part of a witness's statement or transcripts from a previous case. The Chamber's purpose in limiting the number of documents that can be tendered into evidence through the mentioned rules is to have the clearest possible presentation of evidence. In most cases this is achieved by presenting the documents to the witness in court which allows the witness to explain and comment on them. The Chamber prefers this method of tendering documents. However, the tendering of documents together with witness statements will, under certain circumstances, not disturb the clarity of the presentation of a party's evidence. This is the case, for example, with photographs, maps, sketches drawn by the witness, and other similar illustrations of the content of the statement as well as shorter documents clearly referred to and explained in the witness's statement. Further, with regard to associated exhibits, the Chamber expects the parties to carefully consider the need for each document they tender. The Prosecution gave the example of David Harland through whom it wishes to tender 35 documents pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The Chamber has reviewed some of the documents and provide the Prosecution with the following observations: Document number 16 is a 21-page UNPROFOR report drafted by the witness. In paragraph 171 of his statement the witness summarises the content of his report, describing the situation in Sarajevo and other places in March 1995. If the information from the report which the Prosecution would like to bring to the Chamber's attention is that which is contained at paragraph 171 of the statement already, there should be no need to introduce the report as well. In this respect, the Chamber emphasises that the parties should not flood the Chamber with material during their case in chief with a view to anticipating and pre-emptively responding to all possible opposing evidence. Should the Defence wish to challenge the description in paragraph 171 as incorrectly reflecting the report, it may of course tender the report during cross-examination or the Prosecution might do so during re-examination. If there is something else in the report that the Prosecution would like to draw the Chamber's attention to, the appropriate way to do so would be through the witness in court. Otherwise, the Chamber is left to review the report on its own without any clear identification of what is on these 21 pages that the Prosecution finds important for its case, other than what is already found in the statement of the witness. The Chamber has similar reservations regarding, for example, document number 1, which the witness deals with in paragraphs 47 and 48 of his statement; and document number 6, which the witness quotes from and comments upon at paragraphs 91 through 94. In sum, the Chamber will consider any request for admission of associated exhibits pursuant to Rule 92 bis, ter, and quater, regardless of the exact number. The Chamber will carefully consider whether each document is necessary for the appreciation of the witness's evidence and it expects the parties to do the same prior to making their requests. This concludes the Chamber's additional clarification and amendment to the guidance on tendering and presentation of evidence. I move on to my next procedural agenda which is court hearings this week. As far as we can see now, for today and for tomorrow we would sit in the afternoon, starting at 1.00, whereas the Chamber intends and also based on the latest information we've received seems to be able to proceed in this way, the Chamber intends to sit on Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday from 9.00 in the morning until 1.45 p.m. Would this cause any problem for either Prosecution or Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Not for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any problem for the Defence, today and tomorrow afternoon Wednesday, Thursday, Friday in the morning hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Not at all, not a problem for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move to my next item, which is a Defence motion to adjourn the trial or, in the alternative, to reconsider the amended guidance on the tendering and presentation of evidence, a motion which was filed on the 9th of July, that is, this morning. If the Prosecution would want to respond orally, then it has an opportunity to do so. If you would prefer, however, Mr. Groome, to respond in writing, could you then indicate to the Chamber when you would expect to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is one of four motions filed today by the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- I'll start with this one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I would be prepared to answer or make oral submissions on the Prosecution's position tomorrow morning. I would note with respect to this particular one, it does not implicate the evidence of the first witness, Mr. Pasic, in any way, with the Prosecution intends to lead his evidence viva voce. So it would be the Prosecution's position that there is nothing to prevent us from proceeding with the evidence of the first witness at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, anything in response to this request by the Prosecution to respond tomorrow orally?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, we don't have any problem with that either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome, we did not misunderstood you when we thought that you would give your oral submissions tomorrow in the afternoon because tomorrow morning we're not sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Yes, as soon as we start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is hereby clarified. Then I move on to another motion which was also filed today; that is, the Defence motion seeking to adjourn the cross-examination of Richard Dannatt for 90 days. That would be included in your oral submissions of tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll be prepared with respect to all of the four motions tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It may be, Mr. Lukic, that the Chamber would not decide on a motion to adjourn the cross-examination until after we've heard the examination-in-chief. We'll first hear the response tomorrow by Mr. Groome and then we'll further decide how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, at this moment, one more thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Regarding the fourth motion, the Defence motion in limine to bar the use of 65 ter 04472. I heard from the Prosecution that they don't intend to use this exhibit at all, so it may be that it wouldn't be necessary for them to respond to this one in length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I take it if that's the situation it will be a very brief response.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution -- that particular exhibit is not on the list of exhibits announced for this witness. I've explained to Mr. Lukic it's not my intention to tender that exhibit in the examination-in-chief and that I find it difficult to imagine a scenario where I would seek to do so in re-direct, and just to say that Mr. Lukic -- I would encourage him to make a phone call on such matters and it could have been handled without troubling the Court with a formal motion on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from making the observation you just made, Mr. Lukic, is there any reason to withdraw one of your four motions of this morning, in view of information you received meanwhile?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we may decide about it tomorrow morning as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please inform Chamber staff before the start of tomorrow's afternoon session so that we do not waste time in court on responding to motions which you do not want to further pursue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When we are talking about four motions, I think I mentioned the second already, that's the adjourn the cross-examination of Richard Dannatt for 90 days. The third one is the urgent request from the Defence seeking an order barring the Prosecution from using or tendering unlisted exhibits with Witness Harland, and the fourth is the urgent order to bar the Prosecution from using or tendering a document which Harland mentions in his statement. Those were the four motions we were talking about, to have that clear on the record. Then I have no other urgent matters to deal with before we start hearing the evidence of the first witness in this case. I'm looking at the parties, if there's nothing to be raised urgently at this moment, is the Prosecution ready to call its first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is ready to call its first witness, Mr. Elvedin Pasic. And may I introduce the Chamber to Ms. Camille Bibles, who will be taking the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Ms. Bibles, in view of the guidance I've just read out, no need, I take it, to draw your attention to the fact that related adjudicated facts are 799 to 801, 803 through 808, 811, and 814.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I will bring the adjudicated facts where I'm limiting my questions of the witness because of those, I will highlight those for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, before the witness enters the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This morning we received one document created by the Prosecution and delivered to us this morning, and it's on the new list from this morning as well for this witness. So we would ask Your Honours to bar the Prosecution to enter this evidence since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what it is. Could Ms. Bibles -- oh, that's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: List of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me have a look. That's -- yes, that's 28320, I think. Yes. Yes, that's the list of people -- yeah. Yes, Ms. Bibles, if Mr. Lukic has major problems with that, would there be any way to elicit this evidence viva voce without the list in writing?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Our intent was to try to expedite that portion of the testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: -- we think that's an efficient way to present that information but we can do that live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's a list of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, my objection is more of a general nature, not to allow this type of acts by the Prosecution in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we think we shouldn't go this way in the future and we should start making -- [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you now oppose this one? Or would you give a kind of shot before the ship -- but think about that. And meanwhile, Mr. Pasic, it would be unpolite not to welcome you into this courtroom. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text will now be handed out to you by the usher. Could I invite you to stand and make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic. Please be seated. Apparently you preferred to give the solemn declaration in English. In what language would you preferably give your testimony, in Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian, as we call it, or also in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will prefer in English, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will prefer in English. Then, Ms. Bibles. You will now first be examined by Ms. Bibles, who's counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Pasic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pasic. Could you please introduce yourself with your name and your age.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Elvedin Pasic. I'm from Hrvacani, Kotor Varos. I'm 34 years old, born June 3rd, 1978.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you tell us if you grew up in Kotor Varos, at least until you were 14 years old?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I grew up at Hrvacani, Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you tell us the size and ethnicity of your village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. My village was located approximately 13 kilometres from Kotor Varos. My village, Hrvacani, was 100 per cent Muslim ethnicity and approximately a hundred houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you tell us where you went to school?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I attended a school in Vrbanjci and finished the seventh grade there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you tell us the ethnicity of your school mates?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: My school in Vrbanjci was full of my friends, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims all together during that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I will limit further examination with respect to the ethnic make-up of this municipality in reliance on adjudicated fact 796.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe for us in the time-period before the conflict in Bosnia what it was like for you as a child to go to school surrounded by others from differing ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, going to school in Vrbanjci I actually had a great time with my friends, Serbs and Croats, at the same time. We had a great time. Before the war, we shared the same classroom, playing basketball, soccer, and all activities. We were actually sharing everything together. For instance, if we had attend activities outside during our class, as a matter of fact I had friends from my surrounding villages will actually borrow their shoes or the shorts. It was great. We had a great time. There was no any animosity whatsoever. We were celebrating holidays together, whether you were a Muslim, a Croat, or a Serb, at that time we were just having a great time and respecting one another.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you tell us roughly in Bosnia where your village was located?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: My village, Hrvacani, was located 13 kilometres, approximately 13 kilometres from Kotor Varos. That is, I would say, northern part of Bosnia looking at from Sarajevo, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you tell us in 1992 who lived with you in your home?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: In 1992 I lived with my father, my mother, and for the time I lived with my sister before she got married.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And after your sister got married, where did she move to?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: My sister moved to Dabovci, where she met her husband at that time, Elvir. And they lived in Dabovci which was located south from my -- close to Vrbanjci, south from Hrvacani.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992 then, how old were you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I was 13 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And when did you turn 14?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: June 3rd, 1978, so June I turned 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like you to think back to being in school during the spring of 1992. Do you recall seeing any military activity around your school?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, before we finished the seventh grade. The first time I noticed the military activity, one day as I finished class I walked out waiting for the bus to pick us up and we noticed a large convoy of heavily equipped military going towards Doboj. And these -- the infantry or the military was equipped with -- seen tanks and the soldiers were waving at us with -- they were olive-green JNA uniforms seen -- it was a long, long line of motorised vehicles too and they were waving at us with the finger like this raised at us as kids. We were waving back like this at that time. I had no idea what this means. And later I learned that we're not supposed to do that so we were going like this or like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, the manner in which the witness is showing his right hand is with a thumb, index, and middle fingers folded under, or, excuse me, extended, and the middle finger and the ring finger are folded under.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As a child, had you seen tanks before?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: This was the first time for me to see a military tank prior to actually -- let me rephrase that. This was the first time for me to see a tank. I never seen it up close until this time, the first time I seen a convoy and then later on I've seen a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether there were villages comprised of Serb ethnicities within inside your village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: As I mentioned before, my village, Hrvacani, was 100 per cent Muslim village and we had two Serb villages located north. One village was Tepici, north from Hrvacani; and the second village Savici, to our east, 100 per cent Serbs; and to our right, to the west, we had Croatian village Plitska, which was located approximately 3 kilometres to our west. Further south we had Dabovici, which was also 100 per cent Muslim village and part of the Dabovici, the hill of Novakovo Brdo, a few houses were Serb houses where the Serbs lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And drawing your attention to May 1992, did you see any unusual activity around these villages, the Serb villages, that is?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. To our left where the Savici, the village, Serb village, was located we've noticed people digging trenches. Our neighbours, they were digging trenches. And to our north or to Tepici also we've noticed people getting ready for something. A lot of movement. As a matter of fact, to our south, close to Novakovo Brdo we've noticed two tanks that came out of the woods located in Novakovo Brdo with an infantry behind it. They were digging trenches and getting ready for something.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And were you and other people in your village curious about what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact after seeing these unusual activities going with our neighbours, people in our village, as a matter of fact, two well-known and rich brothers, Muho and Murat Dugonjic, decided to go and talk to our neighbours from Savici and Tepici and ask them about the activity and what was the reason for them to start digging the trenches and find out the information. They met in the Lolab [phoen] school between where I attended before I went to Vrbanjci, was located between Tepici, Savici, and Hrvacani, Lolab school where I attended to. After they met with some of our neighbours they were informed that the reason for the people, the infantry, and the trenches, they were just preparing for the military exercises from the JNA and not to worry about it. We are neighbours. That nothing should ever happen to us. In the case that we -- something happens, they're our neighbours, they will let us know, but there was nothing to worry about whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And was there a religious occasion celebrated in your village in May or June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, our holiday Bajram -- we were celebrating our holiday Bajram, which I can't remember May or June it fell on. I remember it just -- we were getting ready for -- celebrated -- first day we went to the mosque. I was excited, as being a little boy. I couldn't wait for this holiday because I wanted to get some money from the elderly people because the tradition for Bajram is to -- when we go and pray, perform the prayer in the mosque, I would go -- the little kids would go to elderly people and kiss their hand and then we would get money. So I was excited. I remember clearly when we were in the mosque that our imam says that if anyone had any -- we used to celebrate our holiday by -- in America we use fireworks but in Bosnia people would use any -- if they had any weapons to celebrate, but fire weapons and make any kind of loud noise. So the imam was concerned because he noticed several activities going on with our neighbours that nobody should do anything that would cause or ignite the situation. It was clear that there was something in the air that's going to -- around us, that it's going to happen. So as we came out, I was excited, I was going to kiss the hand to get more money and then after that we would go to our house and go from the house to house, eat sweets, and celebrate the holiday with the family.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Was the -- was Bajram interrupted in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. On our second day we were attacked by our neighbours. The first day as the imam -- the tradition is for imam to walk from the house to house and greet the people. I remember we were following the imam, that's a tradition, and I remember imam coming to my house because my dad invited him. They came to my house and they decided to talk over it and see if they noticed some activities going on. And they gathered the people would follow the imam. If the imam goes from one house to another, they would follow it. So it was noticeable that the war is coming so they were going to -- they gathered in our house to discuss and determine what they're going to do. On the second day of Bajram we were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe for us just briefly what that was like?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the second day - I'm going back to the first day - after the men gathered and decided what they were going to do, me and my mom were actually told by our father to leave home. There was some men in there to decide or count the weapons if anybody had it, to try to defend ourselves. Obviously the war is on the door. And on the second day, the bombs and the shells started landing in our village. We were in our next-door neighbour in the cellar that night when the heavy shelling started and the firing started. We were under -- in the shell with our neighbours, probably six families all together. It was horrible. I remember as a little kid, you know, the closest I was to -- it was during our holidays when we hear the firing in the air and all that. But anything up close and so surreal when the shells were hitting houses and the ground was shaking, I remember we were covered and my mom told us to go ahead and grab the pillows and cover our heads because we were afraid that if the bullets or the shells would land somewhere close so they don't hit us. And the ground was shaking and loud noises coming. I don't recall any information whatsoever if we were offered any ultimatum to surrender any weapons. I also want to mention that my dad was a licenced hunter. He had a licence for the gun. I don't know how many weapons if they were any in the village, but as I remember it, it was horrible that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, were there voices coming to you or voices, any words being spoken during the bombing and the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, we heard an announcement coming from Tepici, which the village was located north of Hrvacani, on a megaphone, the Serbs were calling, Balijas, where is baklavas and halva, we're going to be there soon. They were calling Muho and Murat Dugonjic, two brothers, well-known brothers, Bring us coffee, we'll be there soon. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What did you and your family do?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That night we stayed in the cellar all night, waited until the early morning. I remember we went this house and somebody knocked on the window and it was so loud my mom jumped up and my dad was there with his gun and he said, What are you still doing here? My mom says, What? He says, The village is falling and they're entering the village from the north. You're the only one left in the village, let's move. And my mom -- I guess in the chaos like that, we start going -- the main entrance of the house that we were in. He goes, No, you can't go that way, we have to go through this little window because we're getting shot at from the Novakovo Brdo bridge. My -- part of my village was looking at Novakovo Brdo. That's when we noticed the tanks. And he goes, You can't go that way because the bullets were -- and the shells are coming so we have to go through this window and go behind the houses, and then we're going to go towards Plitska. And I remember one by one he was dragging us through this window and when we start leaving he looked at me and he says, You have to listen to me carefully. You have to follow my orders. When I tell you to run, you're going to run. And I remember my neighbour, she had a little girl, Merima, and she looked at me and she said, Can you please carry her - because she was pregnant - the little girl. She said, I don't care if you rip her arm out, just don't let her go, so ... We left the house and on the other side behind our house there was the field and road, and my dad says to me, We have to cross this road but we're experiencing heavy firing from Tepici and also Novakovo Brdo. Since you guys are the only ones left, everyone else has actually fled the village and gone towards Plitska, be careful. And he told me, You're going to stand here, and we all gathered, and it was probably six families. So we were standing to cross this road and my brother, I've noticed my brother on the other side and he told me, Look at me. Grab the kid. You're going to jump this wall and when you jump this wall, cross the road. Do not under any circumstances go up the street or down the street. Just cross the road, I'll get you. And I don't know, I guess being a kid, when I jumped and I was carrying the little girl I started walking. And he was screaming, No, no, come this way. And as soon as I rolled over I've noticed the bullets were flying and they were just hitting the spot where I was standing with the kid so I was lucky I didn't get hit. But we experienced -- our neighbours, actually, when we were crossing, the mother of the little girl when we came down to this little area where the fire -- the bullets and the shells were not able -- they were not able to reach it because it was facing the Croat village, she turned around and there were holes in her clothes. Luckily the bullets didn't hit anybody, but they were actually -- you can see the bullets in her -- and he asked us, Why did you still -- my brother asked, Why were you still in there? We have to rush because they're coming. They're burning the houses from the north. And that's when we had to go down in the little wood area and we had to stop, and there was another challenge that we faced by this open field. It was so clear so we had to -- again, we had to stop there and pause and we were given instructions by my dad and my brother that -- the distance we had to crawl for approximately a hundred to 200 metres and they were letting us go one by one. And that's another time when I was really terrified because I was watching the people crawl through this field. I've noticed the bullets flying coming from Novakovo Brdo and literally picking up the grass and the ground and luckily nobody got hurt. I mean, the trees there and the branches were coming down and hitting people in the head from the firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, did you later find out that there had been people who stayed behind in your village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we got to the Plitska there were five elderly people left in the village. We were told by family members that they were -- some of them were not able to move. They decided to stay. The others -- well known Ibro, the old guy, the old man who lived on a pension, Ibro Dugonjic, very religious man, he decided not to go, just stay in his house because he says that's his house. And there were approximately five elderly people who stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Without going into great detail, could you tell us where you and your mother -- where you went over the next few months.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: From Hrvacani we went to Plitska, which was Croat village. And short after being there the Serbs attacked that village and we had to move. From there we went to Cirkino Brdo. Some people went to Bilice. It seems like everywhere we -- I don't want to describe. I mean, we were going back and forth to these villages. Everywhere we went to we were not welcomed. Even the people like Cirkino Brdo and Hafinici had signed their loyalty to Serbs, they were afraid to have us. We were not welcome because we were informed if the Serbs find out that anybody from Hrvacani stays there, or if people from Cirkino Brdo are harbouring people from Hrvacani, that they would get killed. So we were not welcome. Everywhere we go, we were pushed. At one point we were just stuck in no man's land in the woods waiting what to do next. So we were just going from villages to villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And at some point -- I'm sorry, let me back up. You said that some people went to different villages. Was there sort of a group of you that were together then?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Plitska when we reached Plitska before they start the shelling in Plitska, we decided to stay there because we didn't know what to do next, except Cirkino Brdo meanwhile signed a loyalty and Hasan Cirkic who had my aunt Zena, the sister, was with us and he came over with his farming tractor and came to pick her up because she was his sister and the other sister from Hrvacani so -- and then he asked us because we were together to join the group. And he says that he has two houses and he's willing to take as many people are willing to go. So we ended up going to Cirkino Brdo with our aunt.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And these were people from Hrvacani?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the people from Hrvacani. Some of us actually didn't have the relatives in Cirkino Brdo and Hrvacani and decided to go straight to Bilice.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I believe I interrupted you when you said there came a point when you were in no man's land?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everywhere seems like at that time when we went to Cirkino Brdo and spent time there, Hasan came us -- one day when we were working on the field help him, you know, just kind of showing that we appreciate. We were working on the fields and he was approached by the Serb soldiers and, you know, they told him if he was -- when they come back if they found out that Cirkino Brdo was harbouring some of the people from Hrvacani, civilians, that they would come and kill them all. We decided that, you know, he didn't specifically say that, you know, you have to leave but then we didn't want to risk anybody from that village, particularly Hasan, after he gave us a harbour at first, the house. We decided to go to Bilice because it seems everywhere we went through we didn't want to cause anybody to suffer on our account, so we were just -- at one point we were stuck. We didn't know what to do. We were in this little wooded area before we decided to go to Bilice, another huge Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you able to stay there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. We -- actually when we got to the Croatian side, Bilice, that's -- they gave us a warm welcome. We entered the village from the east side and that's when I've noticed and I saw my brother and my father and a lot of men that were -- we got separated in Plitska. It looks like they left from Plitska to Bilice before us and they were waiting for us. So we stayed there approximately a month also helping out, appreciating the locals, the Croat family gave us a weekend house and we were helping while we were there. We stayed approximately an hour -- one month, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And why did you leave there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: When we left Bilice the first time we found out -- I'm sorry, we found out that the people were talking and we've noticed the local ones packing up. So we were afraid that there was something going on. We heard that people were saying that Bilice will surrender. And brother came over -- at one point I think the man -- some of the men stayed in Bilice and left, some of them left for Vecici also, but he's the one who informed us that he heard that Bilice will fall, to surrender, and he was urging us to go to Garici, which is another Muslim village, sign a truce, loyalty to the Serbs, and we decided to go to Garici where we had our cousin, Atif, lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you describe for us whether you, during the summer of 1992, you and others returned to your home village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. After noticing that when we left Bilice we were going towards -- we decided before we got to Garici that at one point we decided to return to our village because we were afraid for the sake of the others who signed the loyalty not to cause them -- and we decided at one point people -- civilians from Hrvacani just to go back to our village. And we gather approximately anywhere from 50 to 70 mainly civilians. We decided to walk and just go back to our village, Hrvacani. As we were coming close to our village there was three Serb houses. We came to one point where the two soldiers were -- the Serb soldiers were walking by and stopped us before we got to the village and asked us -- one soldier was holding his stomach like this. They were -- they had AK-47s. One was in a camouflage uniform and I don't know if he was injured or -- and they were asking, Where you balijas are going? And my mom and her friend Razija Dugonjic stepped up and said, We are going back to our home. He goes, Home, where? They said, We're going back to our village, Hrvacani. And he says, There's nothing left there. There's no place, balijas, for you to go other than Turkey. This is Serbia. How are you going to manage to survive there? There's nothing there left. And Razija responded back, she said, We'll manage somehow. We'll find s way. He goes, I don't care if you get killed. I'm not going to be responsible for that. And then we continued. Shortly after that we reached the southern part of our village.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe for us the condition of your village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I remember clearly when we were coming down and approaching the southern part of my village, I remember that day it was so hot, extremely hot. As we were approaching the two houses, one house belonged to my aunt and cousin. They were completely destroyed. There were two chimneys standing up and just the walls. The smell and just the whole thing just really scared me. When we got there to these houses I remember there was nothing. Everything was burned. Where my aunt's house was, that's where our barn was, it was completely burnt to the ground. There was nothing. We noticed as we were approaching a few cows shot, and they were just bloated and the smell was horrible. And the people -- my aunt she didn't even want to come close, go near the house as we were walking by and just the walls were there and two chimneys. And we continued up because we wanted to see our house. The people just automatically as soon as we got to the village they scattered, people just running to try to see if they can find anything to different houses. I remember I went with my mom. I was running this little path a shortcut, you can go around it, the main street, but there is a little shortcut that you can go to my house and I remember as a kid just running up and down. It was all -- I still, you know, before to me that little hill was so big and, you know, I just crossed it, I was so excited, I wanted to go and see my dog. My dad had a dog. So when we got to the house, the house was burnt completely. Nothing was left there. We had the fridge, the TVs, everything was gone. The walls, what's left of the walls was stripped. We had -- I remember my dad before the war, I helped him to build this -- the wooden panels around the room, the living room, I remember working with him clearly on that, that was all gone. It was not burned. All the furniture that we had, it was completely gone. My dog after being there a little bit, I went -- I was excited because I knew we left the dog on the chain. It was shot. I found him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, in reliance on adjudicated facts 816 and 819, I will not elicit additional testimony regarding those facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, did you find what had happened to the elderly people who had stayed behind?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: After spending, I don't know, I think it was an hour or so trying to gather if we were able to find anything, I was more concerned about dog -- going back. And after I found that, I came back, running back to mom, and said, They killed the dog. And we had a lot of bees also and they were gone too. So we were trying to find anything. Even the food. So I went in, I was looking for honey. I used to help my dad. Everything was gone. And mom says, you know, after a while we were looking for anything. We left -- when we left nobody knew that this is was going to happen that's -- even though we've seen the activities before, we didn't get enough, the clothes or anything, so we left some of the bags actually dug in the holes and they were gone completely. So we couldn't find anything. After a while we decided to go and meet in the centre of the village and we noticed our -- the friends and the family members from Dugonjic, they were crying and mom was crying and she -- and I asked mom, Why is she crying, because I thought somebody did something. She said they found Ibro Dugonjic, the old man was burnt, they found the body. And the little kid was crying because they decided to bury whatever was left of him. And then, so after that, we found out the rest of the people that stayed there were also dead, except one I think was shot dead, but all the other ones were burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What happened to their bodies?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Family members buried them, whatever was left of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you able to stay in your village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: After spending some time there, I wanted to -- when we were in the crossroad in the middle of the village I wanted to see the mosque. We were told not to go because we were afraid of the shelling. I know the mosque itself suffered from the shelling but the minaret did not. We were informed that it was destroyed by hand. So I wanted to go because there's steps that go up to the mosque, and mom says, Don't go there, because they were afraid if the explosive or anything was left there. So we decided to go to the northern side of the village, and then after staying there we decided after experiencing and not finding enough of anything to live there, my mom decided to go straight to Garici. Some of the family members decided, I think five to six families, they didn't have the relatives in Garici and another little Muslim village, Vakufci, also signed loyalty and decided to stay in Hrvacani. We were standing there to determine, you know -- some people started cleaning up, the family that decided to stay there, the mess and try to gather whatever was left. And my mom was determined that we go. There was absolutely no -- then we noticed because on the northern part of our village you can see the part of Tepici, the road that comes down, we noticed a tractor-trailer coming down with the soldiers. And at that point we didn't know what to do so. We were just there. And I remember that the smell of the village just the burn and everything, the family -- my mom gave me a rag or something to put over. She said, Don't breathe, that's because it was really bad odours and smell in the area. And after they reached down and came over these men were fully armed, they were Serbs, some of them mom recognised one of them I think from Tepici, Boro. His name was Boro, I don't know -- I don't recall his last name. And a lot -- I would say 15 approximately, they had some masks over their heads. The others wore camouflage uniforms. I noticed the cross with four C's. They were singing. They had AK-47s and some of them had also olive -- green olive JNA uniforms. One of them stepped out of the tractor and asked us, What are your balijas doing here? And that's when we informed them that some of us are willing to stay in the village and some of us would like to go to Garici, and the others were cursing at us. And then we decided after the exchanging of the information they were -- it was so hot, extremely hot, I remember, and we asked for water and this guy came down from the tractor and he told the other soldiers to go get a bucket of water from the Tepici. So this lasted around 10 to 15 minutes for him to go and come back and I know that we were just drinking that water. Also we had in the group, I remember clearly we had a woman who was carrying a baby or about to give birth and I know she fainted and they wanted water and were asking, What's wrong with her? And the other woman responded that she's carrying a baby and she was about to give birth because she was having the pains. I remember they were giving her water and trying to cool her down. They were really -- told us there's no place for us other than Turkey. We shouldn't be here. They're not going to guarantee us any safety if we stay. And at that moment we asked them if we could go on to Garici.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, go on to Garici?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we decided to go -- the six families ended up staying and we were going down passing through the middle school or the little school I attended and then we were going up to the village, the Serb village, the Savici. As we were approaching the village, the civilians - and I clearly remember this - the civilian Dalibor is the friend or my Serb friend from school, his mom, I don't recall her name now, I'm sorry, but she was really upset. She was dressed black and the other civilians were waiting for us there. And she was really screaming and we were accompanied by two soldiers and she grabbed -- she was trying to grab the gun from this soldier and she was screaming and yelling, Why you balijas wandering around here? There's no place while our soldiers are dying at Vecici you have guts to come and walk through our village. And she was, Give me that gun, give me that gun, I want to kill them all. I remember I was going behind my mom and I was hiding behind her and the soldier pushed her and we continued and they were cursing at us and spitting at us and then we continued towards the Vakufci and Garici.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: At some point did you find yourself going to Vecici?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. After being a while, I would say a month or so being in Garici, we were -- one night I remember we were sitting in Atif's house watching -- since they signed a loyalty to Serbs. We were watching their TV. It was one of the channels. We were sitting there and somebody knocked on the door really loud and we were afraid and terrified. The two soldiers were standing there fully armed, the Serb soldiers. And at that moment a guy just walks in, jumps, and he was my cousin Atif, jumps in, he was really untidy, he had a beard and just looked like a mess. He had a -- he was armed and he sat down with us and says, I'm here, let's have a coffee. And we were shocked because we didn't know what to respond to that. He goes, Give me coffee. Let's have a coffee. I'm here now. And my mom asked him, What are you doing here? Oh, don't worry about it. Those are my friends there outside. Don't worry about it. I'm here to inform you that tomorrow you all are going to -- the civilians who are from Hrvacani who are located in Garici and Vakufci, go to Vrbanjci, get travel documents and after that you will go to Vecici. And he had a coffee and just took off and had -- sat in a car and they took off. And he informed my mom, You will just gather all together and just go down and go straight, because we signed a truce with the Serbs, you should be -- shouldn't be touched at all or harmed. You go to the school and they will issue you travel document and then you will come to Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You've described that he said: Don't worry about it, those are my friends outside. Did you see who was outside?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I've just noticed two soldiers, I don't know if they were actually his friends or he was just -- my cousin he is always kind of hyper and jokes around. I don't know if he meant knowing them or -- but I just noticed that they were fully dressed in camouflage uniform with AK-47s. They were waiting for him outside. They were just the guards on the door waiting for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Where did you, in fact, get your travelling papers?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That morning we woke up and gathered all the civilians. I know there was a lot of us and we went down passing through Dabovici and then went to Vrbanjci. And as we approached Vrbanjci in the school where I attended my seventh grade, there was so many soldiers there. Wow. As we got there -- Vrbanjci, there was the old school and the new school. I attended the new school and that school was completely transformed into barracks. That's how many -- I've noticed also when we were approaching there was an old tank. I learned they were T-55s that was parked right there on the side road because I remember right across I used to go when I was in school there was a little shop I used to get my sandwich there. So it was parked there. So we went, my mom and I think Razija Dugonjic went to the school to get the documents. We were on the side and the soldiers were walking by calling us balijas and cursing at us. At one point I think one of the soldiers my mom came back and before we start walking towards Vecici he asked about -- he recognised my mom and I think he was from Savici, I don't recall his name, but asked about the dad, where is -- he asked -- oh, Mina was my mom's name, Where is Ahmet, where is he now? Is he on the other side? And I don't know if mom responded. I think she just -- I remember her head was just down like this. And short after that we slowly were walking. It took us 20 to 30 minutes to cross to Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll ask if this is about the time when we would be taking a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is about the time, after one hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take a break. Mr. Pasic, the Chamber observed that it's now and then emotional for you to give your testimony. We also observed that you apparently were able to cope with it. If you at any point in time you feel you would need a short break or that you are not able to cope with it anymore, don't hesitate to address me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be escorted into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Pasic. Is there some water in front of you if you would want to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- take a sip of water, don't hesitate to do that. Ms. Bibles, would you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, before we go back into your testimony, I've noticed that you're reading the transcript in front of you. I would let you know that you don't need to worry about the transcript and as soon as you have heard and understood my question you can go ahead and answer.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to go now forward in time from where we broke at the break to the 2nd of November, 1992, when you were with your mother and your father in Vecici. Do you recall a discussion between your parents about how you were going to leave Vecici?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I remember clearly second night when we arrived to Vecici my father came up to my mom and they were talking, I was far away from them, and they were -- I heard them, they were mentioning my name and then I got close and my father was telling me -- telling my mom that he's -- they are leaving -- some of the men will leave the Vecici that night and that he's concerned about my safety being with the mom and civilians staying there so he came -- he actually left and this is when he came back to get me because he was concerned about my safety. He heard from the people that the convoys before that left from Bilice and surroundings, that they were taking boys from the convoys and away from the moms and civilians. So he was concerned about my safety so he came back to get me and asked my mom if -- that he is going to take me to go with them, the rest of the men, to the safe paths -- through the safe passage to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And at this point were all of the Muslims going to leave Vecici one way or another?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to go back. When we got to Vecici my first day, you know, I spent some time after being away from my father a little bit and just -- because they signed the truce with the Serbs for five days, I believe. There were no shelling and the shelling and bombing, nothing, was going on. So we were able to kind of -- he took me around and just showed me the different areas where he was located. We were able to walk through the village. He says that they would never walk during the day, their walking time was the night, but that there were actually agreements -- actually the truce was signed for five days with no firing or the shelling. So that night or the second night the -- I guess the agreement was for the civilians, all the civilians located in Vecici, to surrender and all the men to leave the Vecici for -- towards Travnik safe passage. Because, as I mentioned before, the concern was about any male being -- surrendering to the Serbs would be detained or taken away from the families, either Banja Luka or Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just interrupt, Madam Bibles. When you first asked Mr. Pasic you said you'd like to move forward in time --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- to November. When he answered he said on the second day after we arrived in Vecici. I just want to be sure, are you on the same wavelength?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What date did you arrive in Vecici?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I don't have idea, I don't remember the date exactly when we arrived. I know I spent the day -- first day there and I had a tour of the village, my dad showed me. So we spent the day there. I believe it was the second day. I don't know if the 2nd of November, but at that time I have -- I don't recall not knowing the month or anything. I still don't remember. But I know it was the second day for me to be in Vecici in the house, that's the second day. I don't know if that was the date, actual date that -- I don't remember that. I just remember my second day being there, that we were -- I've noticed my dad had a conversation with my mom to take me away with him instead of going and -- with mom.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And did you -- at what point did you leave Vecici ? Was it that same -- that second night?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. The second night -- that night after they had a conversation and final father decided to take me, and I remember him clearly approached my mom and he hugged my mom and kissed her and told her that, If I ever done anything to you in the past or during our marriage time, if I did any harm to you, I want you to forgive me because this is a long path, long way to go. We don't know what's going to happen, there's a lot of people travelling. I want you to forgive me in any way. And I remember my mom kind of pushed him, she said, Don't say that, you will survive.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Would Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take your time, Mr. Pasic, and indicate to Ms. Bibles if you're ready to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will take this time to refer the Chamber to adjudicated fact 803 that refers to the date. It was the night between November 2nd and 3rd when the men left Vecici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And my mom told him, Don't say that, you're all going to survive. Don't say that. I remember I held my father's hand and that's when we left. It was approximately 8.00 p.m. that night when I took -- he grabbed me by hand and we started slowly walking. I would assume just knowing village that would be north, going towards the little village, Serb village of Staza. I had -- I remember clearly that night it was a clear night, I had a jacket, light jacket on, so I don't remember carrying any food. I think my dad had something like a smoked beef or something in the pocket and we took off that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Was it just men in your group?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: There were also ten women, whom -- two of whom I think were really young, also five to six boys my age. Because when we joined this long group, I don't know exactly how many but I know we started walking and it was uphill we were walking one by one, and as we joined the group my dad told me, You hold my hand, and we were trying to stay all the last name or the cousins together. I remember he just said hold the hand and as people were passing by or joined the group that's when I noticed some women and children also with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you describe what the land or the terrain was like that you were going through?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: As we were approaching the village, the Staza, little Serb village, it was vacant, there was nothing there. The houses were completely vacant. It was the hill-side. I remember my dad was just pulling me constantly. At first I managed to walk and it was just the woods and uneven terrain. Some -- there were some areas where we literally have to hold -- we were holding our hands because it was that steep. So I heard the people just like falling, like slipping, falling, and the word was if somebody sits behind or gets injured, you don't try to help, you just keep on moving until you're instructed to stop. We were going through the woods. I don't remember. I just remember it was clear night and it was -- it was uphill constantly, just -- to me it was just like climbing and climbing and it was so tough, and I remember I was so exhausted but my dad kept pushing me and just pulling me by hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And while you were with your father did something happen that frightened you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: At one point, I would assume it was around midnight, I remember that night, we had people walking by, I don't know if they were -- I guess they were sending a message constantly somebody would walk by because this was a huge line and they would say at one point, you know, they would say, Okay, we have to hurry, or, We have to slow down. So I guess they were sending a message. And at one point I remember somebody walked by and says, He needs to have a different jacket, because the jacket that I had it was like white, and since it was clear they were afraid that somebody can see us at night. So they gave me this giant coat that was all the way down to my ankles and I put it on and it was so heavy so I had to carry that. And I think it was around midnight when the group suddenly stopped and we were instructed just, Hush, hush. And I remember my dad was in front of me and my uncle was behind me so we couldn't move and they're like, The Serbs are close. We're very close to the Serbs. Don't move. Don't make any sounds. I guess being such a large group you can hear people whether they're dropping something. And soon after that the seconds just -- that's when the firing and the bullets start flying from our direction. We were turned faced that way and I was so shocked. I was exposed to the shelling before but I was in the cellar, but nothing up close like that. I was seeing the bullets flying and they were -- as a little kid I would go in a field and catch these flies, fire flies. You know, I thought they were flies. I was trying to catch them because I have no idea that they were bullets. I'm trying to catch it because they were, like, lit up. And my dad grabbed me and we were instructed to lay down and he grabbed me and back of my memory and he shoved me under this giant tree and told me to stay there and it lasted I think an hour or so, just heavy firing. And soon after that stopped quite, you know, a little bit, my dad was calling my name and I was trying to get out of this tree, pushing the branches, but I couldn't get out of it. So finally he called me and he was yelling, and I reunited with him and he found me, pulled me out and we just laid there this time it starts -- the rain was coming down and they were like -- there were no bullets after that. It quieted down completely. And somebody was asking us if the volunteers would get up. There was some people dead. Soon after that I found out it was Ahmet Zec from Vecici and his son who was shot and killed from the ambush. And they were asking for volunteers to go and try to move the bodies or at least, you know, bury them somewhere or do something, and I know my dad was just -- he was leaning on this -- it was like a rock and I was just so tired and I just grabbed his legs and I was just laying down and I think somebody got up from the group and went and removed the bodies from the path under this tree and put branches and covered it. We stayed there a little bit and found out that the group was -- this long group was cut in half and we didn't know where the other half of the group was gone. So after a while being there, I think by this time it was getting around 4.00 in the morning when we finally reunited. Somebody from the group went out in search and found the other group and we reunited together and we came up to this open field with the grass, a lot of grass, and it was so nice. I was so thirsty. I asked my dad, I said, Can you find me some water? And he says, Let me go and look around. So I stayed with my uncle. And I think this field had cattle or something so there was like a little hole from I guess from cattle stepping in the hoof. He found the water from the rain and I remember going there and he says, I don't know if it's clear enough. But I didn't care. I just needed some water. So I went and laid down and had some water from there. While the people were gathering and trying to regroup they were constantly walking around and asking the volunteers to form a lookout and go and look out for Serbs because obviously we were followed. Later on I found out, and I've seen it with my eyes, we had a person who was like contacting collaborating with the Serbs. And they were asking for people when we were laying down all of us just exhausted to form a line or look out for Serbs. And short after that, that's -- somebody came from the group and says the Serbs are all around, we're surrounded. And that's when the firing started again and the chaos everywhere. So we started running close to our -- my dad was -- the leader, Besim, who knew the path to safe -- to Travnik and my dad was constantly just pushing because he knew that he knows a path, to follow him. So that's when -- I believe the mountain was called Jezica, that's where we ended up and the heavy fighting started and the bullets were flying everywhere and I remember my dad says, Go, go, and he grabbed me. He was running down and we were on this hill. And some people decided to fight back, I think 20 to 30 men stood up. He constantly just told me to go and run down. And we were going down this hill, and it was so steep at one point I had to -- I had to -- I was literally sliding because I couldn't walk. And then all this time the firing was coming from our back where it started, so we were down -- going down this steep hill and dad was constantly behind me just trying to shield me. And he -- at one point as we were getting close down to this -- the valley or where the river was going through, I was so exhausted from this coat that I asked my dad, I said, Can you please wait, I have to take it off. I said, It's stuck. And I was sitting there and while I'm doing it, the bullets were just -- it seems like every tree that you go to hide it seems like the bullet was there hitting the tree. So I ducked down and I was trying to get this coat and it was stuck and maybe God wanted to be like that. After that there were people who passed us close to this river. There were mines. They land on the mines including Besim and they were injured. Approximately 10 people died from the mines and I was still stuck on this and then finally I got this coat off me and we didn't know at first that it was the minefield. We thought that they were from that side. So we started running up the hill again with the chaos everywhere and we couldn't because it was so tough to try because it was like sand and sliding. And we stopped there a moment and somebody yelled, It's the mines. We're okay. We can cross the river. When we were walking by -- when I walked by, I saw Besim, his legs were blown away and he was crying and yelling, Give me something, kill me, just -- my dad grabbed me and says, Don't look. We were trying to jump over this river. To me it looked big, I don't know, but we had to jump over it to go on the other side. And I remember it was a waterfall and we had to jump down in that river first in order to cross it, and there were people that were injured, some injured, some dead, they were calling. And I remember Besim was saying, Give me something, kill me. And I think they left him something later. When we were on the other side we heard the gun-shot. I think he killed himself. When we crossed the river we started going up this -- the other hill and we came to a little levelled area and that's when we -- the group of approximately 200 people were gathered with imam and were just taking a break there. Imam from Vecici, hodza, he gathered us all together and said to us, Let us pray, kids, let us pray. We gathered and gathered our hands together and we were just -- ducked under this -- I don't know if it was like the flat area when we were sitting there. We were so soaked. And after that we've noticed the firing was going on on the other side, on the hill, and at one point it stopped. And I remember clearly seeing -- there were probably like 15, 20 men, they were waving at us, and we were so terrified by this point. It was -- we didn't know who was who, which -- I wish we would have went that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, if you would prefer to have a short break, then please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take a short break and everyone should remain standby. --- Break taken at 3.26 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, we would like to restart so if you would stop your conversation. Are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. Mr. Pasic, again, if you need any timeout or anything, don't hesitate to ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, Your Honour, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, don't apologise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I'd like to go back and start with the group that you were talking about, the group of 200. At some point did your group decide to surrender?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. After we performed the prayer with imam, we were sitting and discussing what should we do. As I mentioned, we noticed on the other side of the hill people, the men were waving at us. We were not sure if there was -- were Serbs or part of our group, so we were sitting there and we decided -- we were talking what to do, what is the -- what should we do next and one of the options was either just to go and face them, go on the other side of the hill, which we -- meanwhile while we were sitting there and talking, discussing what we should do, we heard megaphones and announcement going -- saying, Balijas, surrender. If you surrender, you'll live. And if you don't, you all going to die. So we decided to -- that was one option, to go and try to confront them, and the other option was to go and surrender. And some people were resistant on that, and as soon as we mentioned the surrender then this guy who was with us collaborating, Zec, he jumped up and he says, I can arrange that, that's not a problem and he just left this area and he was gone. After a few minutes he came back and he says, I've talked to some of the Serbs. They've guaranteed us if we surrender there should be no harm and we all should be transported safely to Travnik. And at that moment my dad and I and most of us got up and we started slowly walking. There was a little path towards this tunnel. I clearly remember the tunnel. It was approximately 50 metres long. We walk in that tunnel and I remember from the rain had holes in it and it was dripping down and I was so thirsty I was trying to catch the water and trying to have some sip of water. We laid down and I remember we counted each other, approximately 200, and we were in that tunnel and I think the Serb forces noticed that we were in the tunnel, so as soon as we were in there we noticed the bullets were on both in and out on both entrances were heavy firing. And this guy, I remember, Zec, got up and he says -- he ripped his shirt, he had a white shirt on and put it on a stick, and then he says, If you follow me, then we'll go and it's arranged. And I remember seeing -- my dad was there, I was there, my uncles, my sister's husband, my cousins, a lot of people from Hrvacani surrounding, Vecici also. I don't know, but around 200. And we slowly walked towards the Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As you came out of the tunnel can you describe for us what you saw outside?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Certainly. As we left the tunnel, we were walking one by one in a row, straight line. And as we were -- it was like a wooded area and we approached this little field, and we noticed the trench with the Serb -- three or four soldiers came out of there and they were screaming. And they had automatic weapons and they started firing as soon as we approached. We were instructed to -- any man -- anyone in the group acquiring or holding a weapon or anything to raise their hands like this with the weapon and to start slowly walking.
