As we were approaching this trench they told us, All the weapons on the left-hand side and all the belongings, valuables, on the right-hand side. If we find a needle, we'll kill you. And I remember my dad, and I think the entire group of people that went for Travnik or tried to escape to Travnik, had a lot of money because the civilians or the rest of families expected us to make it through Travnik so a lot of men had a lot of valuables, including a lot of money because women were afraid to take it because of finding out that they were -- the Serb forces in Banja Luka and Skender Vakuf they were stripping down everybody to -- and asking for the gold, money, and other things. So my dad had money, my mom gave him money, Deutschemarks, to dad hoping that we're going to go through. And I think a lot of other families did the same thing. So as we were walking down slowly I noticed the weapons on our left-hand side and the valuables, including a lot of money. I've seen a lot of money and they were mainly Deutschemarks. So we were instructed to leave everything and just follow the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe the uniforms of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were camouflaged uniforms and they were -- had AK-47s. I've seen the insignias with the cross and four C's, but they were all camouflage. I did not see any civilian uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you know or recognise any of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I didn't remember any of them, and as far as by name, but I've seen a lot of them joining as we were coming down to this level where they -- afterwards they instructed us to lay down. I know they were joining from different parts of the village. And as we approached to this level ground where it was so muddy and had a water in there I assume from the rain, we were instructed to form three lines. And I was in the third line and we were instructed to form the lines and lay flat, face down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt, Ms. Bibles. Sir, you mentioned a few minutes ago that as you were moving into a tunnel there were bullets coming from both sides. Did these bullets strike anybody in your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. As a matter of fact, I think once they learned that we were in there, to keep us from fleeing the tunnel they were firing, but as soon as the shirt or the flag the guy raised that they stopped and we were instructed to follow the line. At that moment the firing -- but nobody was hurt from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Once you were on the ground, can you describe for us what the soldiers did?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Certainly. When we were instructed to form three lines and to lay down in this puddle of mud and water, I was laying down next to -- my dad was on my left-hand side and my uncle was on my right-hand side. And that's when the Serbs ordered us to lay down face down and I -- start questioning -- picking out the different people from the group including my father. They were really celebrating. They were really excited. The guns were -- literally I could feel the bullets flying over my head. They were firing. Meanwhile while we were face down I heard that the trucks were approaching and more soldiers -- because as they were unloading they were screaming and yelling, Oh, we got the balijas. And they were picking out the people from the group, including my dad. Before they picked out my dad I remember one from our village was picked up and asked him, the Serb -- because we were so close to them, they were behind us, I heard them asking him, Who's your leader? And he says, this guy says, Besim. And where he's at? He's left in the woods. He's probably dead. And they start laughing. Why don't you go ahead and call him? And he was yelling, Besim, Besim. He was yelling at him. And they start beating him. I heard when he was screaming. And then different soldier picked up my dad because he was right next to him and asked him -- kicked him and asked him, What did you find? Oh, you got the boots. Where did you get these boots? Did you kill one of our soldiers? And my dad says, No, I'm a hunter, licenced hunter, and these are my boots. He goes, Oh, no, balija, you killed one of ours. These are the boots from our soldier. And he says, No. He was screaming loudly. They were hitting him. And then they asked him if he had anybody in the group, and my dad says, No. But he did return, because when we returned, when he came back, he was face down. He constantly kept screaming, Are you okay? Are you okay? And I was just -- I was shocked. I didn't know what -- kept saying, Yes. He says, Are you hurt? I said, No. And I know he was hurt too because he never -- he's a strong man and he would never say stuff like that. But I know he was asking because he was hurt. He came back and laid down next to me. They picked randomly -- the next person they picked up was hodza because I remember his favourite saying, My child. He says, Oh, you're the one with the hat on, you're the one who is in charge. You're responsible for this. And, as he always says, My child, no, I'm not. And they start beating him and I can hear him screaming also. And as I was laying down at one point after they picked up different people to interrogate for different things, they mentioned, they ordered us all the women and children to get up. And at first I didn't want to get up because I was afraid to afraid from my dad. And he told me to get up. I told him, No, I don't want to go without you. He says, Get up. I said, No. And my uncle insisted. He said, Get up. You will survive. That's when I stood up and I was the last boy who got up from that group. As I was walking we were instructed not to look around, just to look in front of you. Don't make any sound. Just follow the group. And as I was walking towards the end, I noticed hodza, he was the only one who was faced up and blood. I didn't see him move or anything. And then we started walking towards Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you first tell us, what is a hodza? What did -- who was he to you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Hodza is hodza -- he was imam from Vecici. He was like a father to all of us. He would always give you and tell you right thing. He was very old man, he was an old man, and always give you -- if nothing, he will always tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: When you stood up, were you able to see who was calling for the women and children to stand up?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I did not because we were ordered to look in front of us, and as I was walking down, I remember I had my head down, and hodza was right here on my right-hand side. That's when I just kind of glanced at him like this, my eyes, and I noticed the blood on his face. I did not see who instructed us to get up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: How many were in the group of women and children that stood up?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I would say ten girls, ten women and five or six boys, all together.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And how many men were left lying on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: We counted ourselves, like I mentioned before, in the tunnel approximately 200, anywhere from 150 to a hundred -- 200.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As you stood up and walked, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: We had this -- I mean, when we got up there was this road, gravel road that joined this road to Grabovica. And we were accompanied by a few soldiers. One of them was actually -- they were all in camouflage uniform. One of them was a female who had a semi-automatic weapon. And I remember clearly we were walking slowly and we were several times we were instructed to, Oh, come on, balija, let's lay down. And we would lay down on the ground first for a few seconds and then they would order us to get up and start running, stop. This happened like five or six times. They ordered us to lay down, get up, run, stop. I remember this woman had -- it was a camouflage uniform. She asked us if we had -- she was holding a cigarette and she asked if we had a match -- oh, that's right, you guys -- you balijas don't have a match because you don't have anything. And out of this group one of my friends from Vecici, one of my boys I know we went to school together, he pulled out a lighter out of his pocket and he goes, I got one. And we all stood there and she says, Okay. And he took it and lit up her cigarette and put it back in the pocket and we continued walking slowly. As we were going through to Grabovica, I've noticed several houses and the people were in front of the houses, civilians, elderly people, they were waiting for us, spitting on us, throwing stones at us, cursing at us, and we were just instructed not to look, just look straight and just slowly walk.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And when you got to Grabovica, where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: We passed through the village and short after we passed through the village I remember there was like a curb. We went around the curb and started walking a small distance. That's when we noticed the school and we were ordered to go across the school to this courtyard, and we stopped there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What did they have you do at the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: It was getting dark and we were ordered to form a line, and as we were forming a line the soldiers were on the other side of us and they were all in their uniforms, camouflage uniforms, had all AK-47, and they just had us in a line. At that moment I was thinking: This is the end. Because they had us lined up, this normally meant execution. So we were just standing there for I think it was like two or three minutes until somebody came and -- this guy came in with a hat. By this time it was a little dark. I could not see his face. But he had a hat, almost like a miner's hat. He had a light on. I assume this was a general or some commander in charge. And he did introduce himself. I don't recall his name. He says hello when he approached and asked us -- told us that, you know, that he is, whatever his name was, and that we women and children will spend the night in the school. He's guaranteeing nothing will happen to us and that -- but our men will pay for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What happened after he said those words?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: After he said that nothing will happen to us, we were instructed to go right across, cross the road, and we went down this little path and the school. From the back side there was stairs, I remember clearly climbing up the stairs, and we entered the school. The school had a -- I assume two levels, but it was the ground level where we walked in and our left-hand side there was a classroom, good side of the classroom. We were all instructed to go in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you free to do what you wanted in the classroom?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: When we got to the classroom, we were ordered to pick a seat, whatever, you know, find a seat. I remember I was in the back, all the way in the back. We were all soaked and so tired. We were accompanied by two guards fully armed. They were sitting at the teacher's desk, I remember. One was in the chair and the other was on the desk. And throughout the night they were taking turns, but we were not free -- we were not able to do whatever we wanted to do. Actually, in order to go and use the restroom we had to raise our hands and we were accompanied by the two guards in order to go. They did offer us that night, the same night, to -- when we noticed later on that night that our -- the rest of the men came to the school, they offered us to go and see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Let's talk about that. Did you see the group of men come to the school, the group of men who had been left on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you were able to see them and exactly what you saw?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. As I mentioned before I was in the classroom all the way in the back. The window was on my left-hand side, the left-hand side which was facing the row which we came from. At some point I don't know exactly the time-frame when we noticed the military trucks. It was dark and I know it poured down rain. It was coming down hard. The headlights -- these men were tied -- their hands were tied behind their back and they were in front of the trucks. That's how I know it was them because we've seen them clearly, the trucks were behind them and the light was hitting them as they were walking. They were brought to the school and I remember they were taken upstairs on the second floor. There was stairs going up and they were right above us in the same school.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you go upstairs to see your father?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, ma'am. As I mentioned before, they did offer us to go and see our men and we had people from classroom -- as a matter of fact, I remember Hajrija Dugonjic, who was a newlywed, to her husband Sead Rahmanovic, she is the one who actually went upstairs and saw her husband. I was afraid. Actually, I didn't want to go because previously experiencing my dad when they offered -- you know, when they asked him earlier if he had anybody in the group and he says no, I was afraid for his safety and my safety, so I didn't go and personally see him. But learning out -- finding out from Hajrija that she went upstairs and she came down. She said -- she was crying. She said that her husband was all blue and he gave her a sign because she asked if they were all there. And she said that he mentioned -- gave her a sign that they were all there and I think there were a couple of other people that same night, they went upstairs to see their relatives. I was afraid. I didn't -- I wish I would have went.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what happened the next morning?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I remember the night, there was a lot of footsteps going up and down. We can hear them. We didn't hear any major sounds or anything. As a matter of fact, also that same night when we were in the classroom, one of the Serb soldiers was fully armed to his teeth, he came in, he says -- he mentions that he was captured in Vecici and he noticed this girl was sitting in front of him and ask her -- I guess they went to school together, recognised her, and asked her what she was doing. And he offered her and told her nothing's going to happen to her. You know, he was giving her candy and water, treated her fairly. But that morning when we woke up we were trying to sleep, I remember I was trying to sleep. I was so cold because my clothes were so wet. And we woke up and they told us that we are going for Travnik, that there is two buses waiting for us outside and we have to follow the instructions, in other words, we were leaving the school, the classroom on the back side where we came in. The fence -- we had to go down and we had these angry people waiting for us. They formed a gauntlet and I remember guard on both sides. They instructed us not to go, not to run, one by one. The bus was I would say 200 metres along waiting on the road, two buses. I don't know why they had two buses. One was waiting for us, and we were instructed to walk slowly towards bus. If you run, they had one guard with the gun pointing at and they will -- and says, I will kill you if you run. You can't run, you have to go slow. We were trying -- we were pushing each other, who is going to go first. Nobody wanted to. I think at some point this little kid who had a match that I mentioned him earlier, he decided to go. And he started walking and as he was -- I think he reached like halfway through, these people had a -- they were so angry, the civilians, all -- they had the sticks, axes, for -- they had -- they hit him I remember just hit him on his knees and he fell, fell down on the ground, couldn't move. And they would let the next one go and as we were going taking a beating through the gauntlet, we were dragging him, trying to take him to the bus. When -- every time when someone pushes me to try to go next I was always trying to avoid so my turn was -- I was one of the last ones. I started walking and I was -- I remember I was like -- my goal was to try to reach that tunnel -- that bus, I'm sorry, the bus and I didn't care about anything else, but I felt a horrible beating on my back and I was just kept walking, just going through there. I didn't care. I just wanted to get to the bus. As I was getting beat up on my back side, all over my body, I don't remember, I was just trying to get to the door. And I was so close, this old lady dressed in black, she grabbed me and pulled me on the ground and had a knife. She put it on my neck. She said, Let me kill one balija because two of my sons died in Vecici. I tried to pull apart. I was trying to pull apart and I was not strong enough. And this guard grabbed her and pushed her aside and he grabbed me and threw me in the bus and he closed the door. And we were told, Sit down, don't look around, and we were all in the seats crying like this. These people for some reason, they tried to start the bus and it wouldn't go. And these people from the gauntlet, they went around the bus and they were shaking the bus and banging on the window, throwing stones, spitting at us, and we were there for a good 10, 15 minutes. I thought they were going to tilt the bus over because they were so angry. And as we -- then finally the bus started and we started -- I turned around, I remember I'll never forget that. I looked up and on my right on the second floor I saw a hand -- there was a hand waving. I didn't see the body but there was a hand waved like this and I see that hand in my dreams.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will refer the Chamber to adjudicated facts 804 through 808 with respect to the findings of previous Trial Chambers and this Chamber with respect to what happened to the men on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we just get clear, second floor of --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Second floor of -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness can tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was in the second floor of the school?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He doesn't know who, he saw a hand, but second floor of what.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As you drove away in the bus you said you saw the hand on the second floor. What was the building?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: When we entered the bus, the school was on the right-hand side and the way -- the arm came from the second floor where our men were left. Like I said, I didn't see the body, but I just seen somebody wave from the second floor of the school that we were in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did the bus that you were in eventually make it to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: As we left Grabovica in the direction we walked -- came from when we were walking, that direction we went back with the bus, the bus in front was an empty bus and we all -- all of us, including the Zec, the guy who was collaborating with the Serbs, he was in there too. We joined the rest of the buses, approximately 13 buses when we approached Vrbanjci. We were the last bus with the rest of the civilians from Vecici. I remember also in the bus that we didn't talk. They told us not to talk about it or talk anything, just look in front of us and that this Zec guy was greeted by these soldiers inside and saying how great job he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you see your mother again?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: As we left Vrbanjci, joined the buses, we took off. I don't know -- I don't remember exactly which direction, but I know we were the Skender Vakuf end of Vlasici. I didn't see my mom in Vrbanjci, but actually I didn't see her until I came to Travnik at all. They had no idea what had happened in Grabovica. They had no idea that we were behind them. When we reached Vlasici, we were ordered to -- they stopped the buses at one point on the Vlasici and told us to get out. And they would let one or two buses at a time and us to stay back. I guess they were giving time for these soldiers to come in and ask for more money. They were jumping out of woods in, like, groups of 10, 15, and asking for -- they had a mask. They were in the camouflage uniforms, but I know every one of them had a mask over the face. Couldn't see the face. They were asking for the money, gold, any valuables, and just stripping us down. Since our bus was the last bus, so we were amongst the last ones who actually left the scene and tried to reach to the safe Bosnian side, I remember every time when we get approached by -- jumped by these people, the soldiers, and asking for belongings, it's unbelievable, people were just lost and standing there. We didn't have anything. They kept asking, Money, money, balijas, give more money, gold. We didn't have anything. At one point, I don't know if I mentioned this, but I'm going back now, I remember I had -- I was approached by the soldier and I had also a knife at one point on my throat and asked if I had money and I said I had nothing. I kept just running trying to catch to my mom because every time I asked somebody in that group, Where is my mom? And the people were just lost. At one point they didn't respond and at one point they were, like, just point out go. And I clearly remember Smetovi is this road. It was so crowded with the belongings that at one point we had to literally had to crawl over the bags and the clothes. You couldn't see the pavement. It was so hard to go through. I think like three or four times we were jumped by these people until we finally reached the Bosnian side. These men came out, the soldiers came out, they were also in the camouflage uniform, and at one point it was just not again, and they were like, No, we're okay. Here's water. You're on the safe. They were waiting with trucks and buses for us to take us to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you asked to look at a list of names of people to see if they were with you either in the tunnel or on the ground before you got to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes. Did you review a list of names of people who may have been with you in the tunnel or on the ground before you reached Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And that was this past weekend?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to -- did you recognise some of the names?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the most efficient way to go over the names of people that he recognised would be to pull up 65 ter 28320 the Defence referred to earlier. I could also just review the names with the witness and have him give a brief description of where he -- if he knew them and where he last saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any problem if the list be shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Grounds, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Grounds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was disclosed late to us. It was disclosed this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that's the sufficient ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, could you tell us whether this list existed before and whether it was disclosed to the Defence and when it was disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness recognised 14 names from the list. He -- we put that into a proofing note with respect to his information. We had it translated into B/C/S on Sunday. I sent an e-mail to the Defence team Sunday, late afternoon with that, and then we provided it this morning along with just a list of the names, which is what we would show in the 65 ter exhibit that does not have the information -- the additional information from the witness. It's just a list of the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I do understand that the list was produced during the proofing session. If you are surprised by any names or if you would like to verify whether there are any names on that which needs to be further researched and if that leads to any results in your research which would justify that further questions would be put to the witness, the Chamber will consider such a request. At the same time, at this moment the Chamber does not oppose this list to be shown to the witness and that the witness be asked whether this is the names that were shown to him and whether he recognised any persons from that list. But again, if there are any persons on that list or any names which caught you by surprise -- because, Ms. Bibles, let me just try to understand, the only purpose of the use of this list is to identify persons who were with the witness during the -- when he left Vecici? Nothing more, nothing less?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, individuals who he last saw either in the tunnel at the time they surrendered or on the ground right after they left the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One second, if I may, I would like to draw your attention to one procedural issue as well. This document is added to 65 ter list without asking Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be my next point. Of course the Prosecution has to ask to add it to the 65 ter list if they would like to proceed in the way they suggest. That goes without saying, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I think they have to ask it before they use it. That's our point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I fully agree with you that that would have been the appropriate procedural approach. At the same time usually if a document is produced at a very late stage, tendering it usually is understood to be -- to include a request for having it added to the 65 ter list. But procedurally, you're perfectly right. Ms. Bibles, may I take it that that is -- it's a two-step story, the one is to ask permission to add it to the 65 ter list and then to use it with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And I was aware because of the proceedings before that this might require some discussion, so I would properly move to add the exhibit to the 65 ter list and then tender it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any further comments, apart from what you commented already, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to stick with our objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'll consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first decision is whether or not leave is granted to add this document to the 65 ter list. Leave is granted, so you can use it if you -- as you deem fit at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would ask the court officer then to bring up 65 ter 28320.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you see the list of names in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you tell us whether this is a list of the people that you identified that you knew?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you tell us where you last saw the people who are on this list?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. Do I need to go over -- say anything about the names or just --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'll go through briefly the names with you. But do you recognise -- did -- when was the last time that you saw the people on this list?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Before it was in the tunnel, some people in the tunnel, and some while we were laying down on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've just looked at the clock and realised this may be a break time. I'll -- I'm happy to go forward and finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I believe less than ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course we had kind of an additional break in between. Perhaps it's better if you would finish in the next ten minutes and then take a break of some 20 minutes and then start cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to briefly go through the list, and if you could tell us approximately if you know how old this person is and just indicate briefly where the last time that you saw them was. The first is Nedzad Menzil.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Nedzad Menzil, he was a year older. His dad -- he actually, when we were praying right before the ambush -- second ambush, he was shot and killed, a year older than I am. I remember him clearly because we were -- as kids we were playing. He was shot and killed, shot in his stomach and I remember his dad covered him with branches and left him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And Opakic Seval.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, Opakic Seval had a brother, also Nedzad. I remember he was probably a couple years older than me. Before the war we used to get comic books from him. I saw him in the tunnel and I remember -- I asked him because he was constantly in Vecici and he was making weird sound when I would talk to him since I didn't see him since Hrvacani the whole -- I saw him in the tunnel and he was making a weird noise, and I said, What happened? And he had a hole in his throat. And he says he got -- when the shell hit the ground when he was in Vecici a piece went in his throat, and every time he would breathe it would make a horrible sound and it would interfere with his voice. So he was in the tunnel with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Pasic Sefik?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Pasic Sefik, my uncle, I remember him also laying down next -- on my right when we were on the ground right before we got up. He had a house right next to us, always treated me as his kid.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Pasic Fadil?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Pasic Fadil, I had four other brothers, one of them was my age. He was the same age as my cousin, Nihad, further cousin from my father's side. We used to play as kids. He had horses so we went horseback riding.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Pasic Mehmedalija?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Pasic Mehmedalija, the father of the little girl that I was carrying in Hrvacani. He was bald. He was there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: In the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Pasic Mustafa?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, Pasic Mustafa was -- he's my cousin from father's side. His house was on the top of the village, the Pasic side. He had a vehicle. Before the war, we used to go as kids when he would lift his vehicle and work on the vehicle help him with the tools.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Where did you last see him?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: He was in the tunnel with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And Pasic Nihad?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Pasic Nihad, my dear friend, my cousin. He was there too in the tunnel. We used to play as kids, take care of our cattle, everything. He was like my brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Pasic Sakib?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Pasic Sakib, my other cousin from father's side. As I mentioned in the previous statement, when we returned to Hrvacani his -- one of the houses at first we'd seen, it was the one on the right, that's his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Where did you last see him?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I seen him in the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Rahmanovic Sead?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Rahmanovic Sead, the husband of Hajrija Dugonjic, who -- newlyweds. I've seen him in the tunnel and also in the school, according to her he was upstairs because I remember clearly that night she went up and saw him. He was there in the school on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Turan Mustafa?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Turan Mustafa, he's from Hrvacani, familiar last name. I don't have any relationship with him, but I know him as a little but I don't have any relation with him. He is definitely from Hrvacani.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And where did you last see him?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: He was in that tunnel before we went down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And did you also last see Turan Namko in the tunnel last?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And Turan Rasim in the tunnel last?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And Dugonjic Murat in the tunnel as well last?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Dugonjic Murat, I think we made a mistake, is the father. His son Muradif in my statement is the son, not the -- Murat is the father. Muradif is his son was with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So that should be Radif?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Muradif, yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Muradif.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: -- as I mention in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And Lihovic Elvir?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Lihovic Elvir, he was there too. I've seen him before in the tunnel, and also down when we were walking down we were close to each other. He's my sister's husband from Dabovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And what is your father's name?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: My father's name Pasic Ahmet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to your father?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, after being there that night, there's no doubt in my mind that they were all killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The rest of these people stayed in Grabovica, and no doubt in my mind that they ended up dying.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Bibles, of course I asked myself whether you want to tender this document, and at the same time I ask myself what would the document add to the testimony of the witness. So even though it's now on the 65 ter list, all of the names are part of the testimony. One of the names is corrected, it might even -- a reason not to have it admitted because there's a correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I would agree. I will withdraw my motion to admit that as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- well, I don't know whether it was already tendered, but at least there's no need to decide on that on the present circumstances. No further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Then I suggest that we take a break, that we resume at 5.00, and that you start your cross-examination at 5.00, Mr. Lukic. Could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we'll resume at 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, could you give us any idea on how much time you'd need for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to fit into 60 per cent of direct time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 60 per cent of direct time which would mean a little bit over one hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One hour and 15 minutes, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if it would be -- of course we'll follow our cross-examination. If it would be possible to make it so concise that we could finish the witness in one hour, that of course would be better --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but we follow you already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to reduce my questions right now so I'll try my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we were scheduled until 6.00, but apparently we're scheduled for 5.45, so therefore I was perhaps asking this question on the wrong assumption. Mr. Pasic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Pasic. [In English] You can answer in English.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us, what was the name of your grandfather?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: My grandfather's name Alipasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were enumerating those names put to you by the Prosecutor a moment ago. Could you tell us those names again quickly without the list?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Sure. I'm going to start with my father, Ahmet Pasic; Nihad Pasic; Mehmedalija Pasic; Mustafa Pasic; Fadil Pasic; Dugonjic Muradif, the son of Murat; Menzil Nedzad; Turan Mustafa; Turan Namko.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next thing I'd like to go through with you quickly is if you could summarise your movement from place to place after you left Hrvacani, and could you tell us how long you stayed in each of them?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Sure. After I went -- left Hrvacani, obviously my first stop was Plitska. I would say day or two or -- don't know approximately. Maybe one day in Plitska. I'm not quite sure, but I just know as soon as we got to Plitska and we were trying together -- I think it was the same day, then the Serb forces started shelling Plitska, so from there we went to -- we actually were trying to decide whether we should go to -- some people went to Bilice and some to Cirkino Brdo. Obviously by then my aunt's brother from Cirkino Brdo, Hasan, came over to pick her up and asked us to go with her because he had two houses. And we -- I would believe that it was the same day that we went with his sister, my aunt, Zena Pasic, and went for Cirkino Brdo. We stayed there I don't know -- I don't remember exactly how many days because travelling from place to place -- we went to Cirkino Brdo, then from Cirkino Brdo --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] So you don't know how long you stayed in Cirkino Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I am going to say maybe two weeks, three weeks. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I mean -- but I know we were there helping Hasan and we worked on the field, so a few days we were there --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. How long did you stay in Bilice?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: After we went from Cirkino Brdo to Bilice, approximately a month we stayed in Bilice before we ended up going back -- try to go -- so I would say a month in Bilice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you went to Hrvacani and how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: In Hrvacani we just -- half a day we stayed there. We tried to stay because we didn't want to go anywhere else to create any trouble for anybody else, we signed a loyalty. So that was the same day that we left for Garici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Garici, how long?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Approximately a month we were in Atif's house helping him out also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you went to Bilice; right? How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That's correct. We went for Bilice. I don't know how many days we stayed there. I know it was days when we went second time back -- that's when my brother came to Bilice and told us that he found out that they were going to surrender and that the best way -- I mean, he was going to take us to Vecici together, but he suggested to go back to Garici because being in Vecici was not safe place for us. So I don't know, few days we were there. I don't know exactly how many days before it fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Garici?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly how many days. I don't remember now, but I know when we went back it was -- I don't know exactly how many days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Several days?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Several days I would say, close to a month. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'd prefer if you would let the witness finish his relatively short answers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vrbanjci, did you just pick up your documents there or did you stay there a while?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: In Vrbanjci we just stayed that same day just to get the documents, and then as soon as mom and the rest of the civilians got the documents, we went to Vecici the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then Vecici again, how many days?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I know that I spent the night there. I know that, that we spent the night because once we met with the father and they determined which direction we should go they -- and then second day we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And before you came to Grabovica, how long did your journey take when you were trying to get through from Vecici before you were arrested in the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I know we left that night, as I mentioned, at 8.00 p.m. We travelled the night and then we were ambushed around midnight, so the following day we gathered together 4.00, around 6.00, 7.00, so we were ambushed second time and lasted entire day. So it was the following day that we managed when we ended up in the tunnel and going --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Two days max; right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, two days max.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you, speaking of Bajram, do you recall if it was Kurban Bajram or was it the Ramadan Bajram?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: You know, I don't remember. I -- if I may assume that it was Kurban Bajram. I don't know. I don't know if it was after fasting or -- Bajram or the one for when we perform the hodza. I am not sure. I don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You speak about the JNA. Was the JNA made up of all ethnicities in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I believe so that the JNA before the war was -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And your brother you say was in the JNA. Was he doing his military service or was he at a military school?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: My brother was in a military school. He did not attend military service. He was in a school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How old was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: He was born 1973, so I don't know, 18, 19, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he in a secondary school or was he attending the military academy?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I think on military academy, that's what ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What secondary school did he finish before that, if you know? Was it also a military school?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No. He finished a school in Vrbanjci and after that, if I may explain, in order to -- military academy after he finished the school in Vrbanjci, he applied. My dad was always -- before the war he wanted him to go and attend the school and of course my mom was against it. But he listened to my dad and he applied and in order to get accepted, it was really -- I remember it was really strict school. Then he would go to Banja Luka and Sarajevo, take extra exams. And he finally got admitted. I know my dad was so proud of him. So he finished the school in Vrbanjci and then after that he was admitted to academy and then he went to -- for Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Earlier today you mentioned also that the men had AK-47s, as you said. Did you know the name of that rifle at the time; and if you did, how?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Since I live in America, that's how I found out AK-47, obviously. But being in Bosnia I know we called them "automatska puska" [Interpretation] Automatic rifle. [In English] And that's how I know AK-47, by living in the states and just being there, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also talked about tanks, that you saw tanks there and you were told that a military exercise was going on. At the time were military columns from Croatia passing by on that road? You said they were going towards Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: The first convoy when I was in a school when we came out, it was JNA, clearly it was JNA and there was no -- I didn't see any insignias or insignia like that, but it was JNA with the star and the tanks and mainly the three fingers, olive greens -- solid olive green uniforms, some camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the fighting started in Kotor Varos municipality and who took Kotor Varos over? At the time did you know?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Clearly when our village was attacked, I don't know exactly what month and I know it was Bajram, the holiday, we were attacked by the Serbs. And as I mentioned before, our neighbours -- noticing the activities in our neighbours, the trenches and all of that, it was the Serb army. I don't know what -- at that time, but it was the Serbs and they controlled the Kotor Varos during that time. They were in the city and controlled most of Kotor Varos until they took it completely over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Serdare village is?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was in Cirkino Brdo it's not far away from Cirkino Brdo. I don't know how far it is from the Hrvacani, but when we were -- took refuge in Cirkino Brdo, not many houses were there. The Serbs also -- I don't know how far the distance-wise, but yeah, I know approximately where they were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you moved around that area, did you see that village burnt, destroyed, people evacuated?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I remember when we were travelling from a place to place and trying to find a home, I don't think -- I was never -- we were never close to that village because most of our moments when we were leaving Hrvacani and going to Cirkino Brdo, Hanifici, Plitska and Bilice, that's way up north so I never had chance to even come close to the village. We were just crossing the hills I think north of that. I never went through the village of Serdare.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just again briefly about your brother. Was your brother called names because he had attended the JNA military academy for a while?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: As I mentioned, my brother, you know, being in academy being away from the home they had a chance to come home only during May. That was the time when we were released from the army and they would spend time with us. So when he came in May to see us, he was fully dressed and it was not the olive green, it was similar to like a bluish and like a pilot. And he was really sharp-looking. And I remember when he -- at this time I think the war in Croatia and Slovenia already started and it's been going on and the people were just -- they start call him by name Chetnik because he was still active in military academy at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we conclude that people from your village called "Chetnik" anyone who wore a JNA uniform regardless of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure to -- I don't know what to answer to that question, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would require anyhow a proper factual basis before drawing conclusions, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I thought that I draw one, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- I'm showing that his brother, being Muslim, was called "Chetnik." That's why -- that was my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and would that be a proper basis to answer a question: Can we conclude that people from your village called 'Chetnik' anyone who wore a JNA uniform ..."? We had one apparently one case where that happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's [overlapping speakers] for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and then we could ask the witness whether he is aware of any other person wearing a uniform being called a Chetnik, and then we might have a broader basis for drawing any conclusions. Are you aware of anyone apart from your brother but wearing a JNA uniform being named "Chetnik" by the people in your village as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I may, I don't remember anybody at that time in the village that was actually attending JNA or was in the JNA except my brother was in the military. So his friends were calling him at that time that name. I don't know, I don't remember if they were calling anybody else or if just because of the uniform, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you feel that there was some animosity towards the JNA in your village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. If I may, before the war JNA -- obviously everyone had to do it. It was the -- we had -- people had to attend JNA before the war and I remember actually several people that were going through JNA. As a matter of fact, when I was little I actually, being in a class we respected Tito, and you know -- there were military exercises way before the war when they actually -- JNA members came in and did exercises in my village, perform. And, you know, I remember as kids going to the mosque and they had blue and the green, the groups, and they were exercising, so we would join and just go with the groups and they would give us, you know, weapons and we would just -- we actually respected the army before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I notice that your answer was focusing on the period before the war. Now Mr. Lukic had not given a clear time-frame for his question. Mr. Lukic, were you interested in how the JNA whether there was any animosity before the war or once -- well, let's say perhaps 1992 when there were problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was no JNA anymore when the war erupted, Your Honour, so I was asking about before war, so he answered my question actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that's clear to me now as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're now saying your father left your home. Did he come back the same night?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: When the shelling started, we were in the cellar, like I -- as I mentioned. And I don't know what happened. He went but I know that same morning or that night we were in the cellar, the morning when he came in and knocked on that window and says, You need to get out --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, we've heard you. Before he came back you say you heard shelling. Did you also hear the sounds of fighting, the sound of rifle fire?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. We heard the shelling and also the bullets -- because the way my village is, as I mentioned, the southern part of the Hrvacani, so I don't know if the shells were coming from Novakovo Brdo or the Savici or Tepici, but the bombs explosion we heard and also the bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you learn how many people got killed from the shelling, how many people were wounded?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: We learned that morning when we escaped to Plitska, as a matter of fact when we got to the house I know for a fact, because I've seen it with my eyes, they -- a man in his -- 30 years old, he was wounded from the shell and he was screaming, screaming and making a noise. And my mom was there and they were looking at him. He had a piece from shell hit him here and they were ask if anyone had anything to try to patch the wound. And they asked this woman who was nursing a kid to try to use her breast milk to put it on the wound. I remember one that was injured from the shell. I don't remember anybody getting killed except the people that stayed in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you went to Cirkino Brdo and you say they had signed a statement of loyalty and nothing happened to them. I have heard so much about this statement of loyalty. Have you ever seen that or was it just talk?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, whether you heard a lot about the statement of loyalty seems not to be very relevant. You would like to know from the witness whether he has seen the statement of loyalty?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then apart from introducing your own experience and observations, ask the witness what you would like to hear from him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Mr. Pasic, have you ever seen anything like a statement of loyalty?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, sir, I never seen any written statements other than when we went to Vrbanjci and we had a piece of paper that was staying from Vecici -- from Vrbanjci to Vecici. But as far as the Cirkino Brdo, I never seen actual document with my eyes, I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The people in Cirkino Brdo were the same ethnic group as you; right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, 100 per cent Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the only difference between them and the residents of Hrvacani was that they did not wage war against the Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: The difference is we were attacked. Hrvacani was attacked. I don't remember them offering us to surrender or lay down if there were any weapons, I don't remember that. As far as the Cirkino Brdo signed loyalty to the Serbs, we know that even when they signed loyalty to the Serbs that Hanifici and Cirkino Brdo a lot of civilians, even when they signed, especially in Hanifici, were burned in the mosque even when they signed. So the guarantee was not a hundred per cent like they promised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you hear about Hanifici? You haven't mentioned that yet?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Now that I'm fully back in that -- during that time, when we were at Cirkino Brdo and helping Hasan to harvest the crop and the food, he were -- he was informed that if he helps the civilians or if people from Hrvacani stay there and if they come back that they might put Cirkino Brdo into great danger. As a matter of fact, one day we were -- I don't know which day but actually we were Cirkino Brdo going to the fields when we heard the screams and people running from Hanifici and since Cirkino Brdo sits above -- higher ground than Hanifici, we noticed that the soldiers were going in and burning houses and people were screaming and they were -- they gathered them together in the mosque and set up the mosque on the fire. That's when we picked up our belongings and we ran towards Plitska again and Bilice running back, including some of the people from Cirkino Brdo. We all ended up again back at Bilice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how many people fell victim in Hanifici, what are you saying to us?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I don't fully remember or seen it, but we just seen the smoke and the mosque coming from that area. I don't know how many casualties were there in the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then later you arrive in Bilice. That's a Croat village; right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The people there were well armed; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: When we approached the Bilice -- I don't know if this was a first or a second time because we were going back and forth, I did -- we entered the sides far away from Kotor Varos. Indeed, I've seen 10 to 15 people with automatic weapons fully armed and they were organised and they had Croat insignia -- or symbols, Croat symbols.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see trenches dug around Bilice?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also military-age men from your village were already in Bilice; right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Most men were there. They were there and we were on an eastern part I think of Bilice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it evident that they were getting ready or that they had already been involved in fighting the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That I do not know. I just know when we entered the village, men including my father, my brother, they were on the part where there was no harm coming other than the part of the Bilice close to the Kotor Varos, that's when we heard the intensive fighting. But on this part there was absolutely nothing because there was no shelling until we spent some time there and then we were shelled also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you arrived in Bilice, your father and brother were already there; right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: People from Hrvacani who were not in Bilice had already left in the direction of Vecici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Some people stayed in Bilice and also some went for Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You found your brother and father in Bilice and then later the two of them went to Vecici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I don't know if this was the second time when we went to Bilice or the first time. I know my dad, either on the first time or the second time, ended up going to Vecici. My brother stayed there, and then I think at one point he was there with us, I know when we were there, and then we left, then we came back. He was gone, but then again he came back when he found out they were going to surrender. So to answer your question, yes, my father left from Bilice for Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you returned to Hrvacani you say 50 to 70 of you all together. And there you encountered two Serb soldiers. One had been wounded and the other one was carrying him. Do you know how that soldier had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: When we approached them, the one standing up was, you know, obviously I mentioned before they asked this question, the other one I didn't see any bleeding, but he was -- I don't know if he was wounded or if he was hurt, but as I mentioned he had his body like this with the gun holding like this and the other guy was holding him. I don't know, I didn't see any bleeding, but it seemed like they were in a big rush. I don't know if it was -- I didn't see any bleeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, sorry to intervene, but the question was whether you know how they were wounded, how they got wounded, I take it. So not what their wounds were, but whether they were shot or whatever happened to them. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I don't know what happened to them. I don't know if they were injured somewhere, but I just remember seeing them there. I don't know if he was wounded at the line or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite you to very much focus on exactly the question that is put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These two soldiers, did they try to stop you from going back to Hrvacani?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: At one point a guy -- one soldier was really angry and he says that, There's no place for you, balija, going back to Hrvacani because your place is in Turkey. And he says, If you go there, we don't -- we're not going to be responsible for if something happens to you. He was cursing at us and then eventually they just took off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As His Honour, Judge Orie, said, please focus on the question. The question was whether they were stopping you from doing that? Did they kill someone? Did they beat somebody up? Did they wound someone? Did they try to stop you in any way from going on to Hrvacani?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying. No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bear with me, Your Honour, just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now you are referring to Hrvacani. A group of soldiers approached you and you say 15 wore masks. The people with the masks, did they have crosses with four S's or were they some other people?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: As I mentioned before, 15 to 20 soldiers. They were not all masked and I don't remember seeing -- I've seen on some of them, not all of them, that they had four S, but they were not all masked. So some of them were and the others were not and I've noticed on some of them -- but they were not all with the four S's.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Some of them had olive-green-grey uniforms and others had camouflage uniforms, that's what you had said, they had taken a tractor. What did they look like to you, like soldiers and army or like a local gang, the way you described them?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I just -- I know that they had a leader, obviously, the one who stepped out to help out with the water. But as far as the -- seemed like they were following the order from this guy, so I don't know if they were army or a gang, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, they hadn't killed anyone, injured anyone, or beaten anyone up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that you went to Garici, to your relatives. Now that we're on the subject of Garici, is it also correct that the inhabitants of Garici stayed on in their houses unhindered up until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you rephrase that question. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Sure. [Interpretation] You went to Garici to your relatives. Is it correct that your relative, like all the other inhabitants of Garici, stayed in their homes until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you went to Garici, for instance, you tried to decide amongst yourselves where it was that you would go. No one issued you any orders, like where you should go?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, as a group being there our goal was to go back there, return to our village. That was -- at first we decided to do that, but after finding out that there is nothing left in there and there is a lot of things in order to survive, so we just between us in the group -- my mom -- and they decided to just leave, and after experienced and seeing the stuff and destruction, we decided just -- among ourselves, there was absolutely nobody in there who forced us or did anything among ourselves to go -- and since we had the group -- majority of the group had relatives in Vakufci and Garici, most of us decided to go in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock. We'll finish for the day. But first, I would like to instruct you, Mr. Pasic, not to speak with anyone about your testimony or to communicate in any other way about your testimony, whether this is testimony given today or testimony still to be given tomorrow. Mr. Lukic, could you give us any impression as where you are, how much time you'd still need tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: More than today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: More than today?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: More than today. I'll try to condense my questions, but I don't know how much time did I spend today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think today you used 45 minutes, close to 45 minutes. You would need more tomorrow, then that would be -- well, that would be even -- well, beyond the 60 per cent instead of within.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How much time do I have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you asked for 60 per cent, isn't it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I get?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After two hours, which is a little bit over one hour, as a matter of fact it's one hour and 12 minutes, if I'm not mistaken. So would you please review your schedule and then perhaps also -- it was not always entirely clear to me what was in dispute and what you challenged. I felt sometimes there was some testing of the reliability and credibility of the witness. Sometimes it was not entirely clear what was in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to state the position of our defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not in the presence of the witness, certainly not. Mr. Pasic, I will ask you to be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back tomorrow at 1.00 in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
